courses.description: English 9 Enrichment is a full year course which meets every day for a full block. Students earn two credits for successful course completion, one elective credit and one English credit. In order to get credit for this class, students need to show mastery of the PBGR proficiencies associated with this class. Students will work to build their reading, writing, and communication skills to gain the background they will need for completion of elective classes during their junior and senior years. Fluency instruction is an important element of the class which students will participate in daily to increase smooth reading and to develop reading speed. The class includes a literature component, in addition to other instruction provided. *Students cannot self-select for enrollment into this course; enrollment is based on team recommendation.

The freshman English program focuses on the analysis and interpretation of fiction and nonfiction while working to develop students’ writing and communication skills as they gain the background needed for completion of elective courses during the junior and senior years. As well as presenting and practicing essential communication and writing skills identified in the Common Core Standards, this course addresses the Vermont state writing benchmarks. * The 9th Grade Honors English course covers the same areas of study but in a faster paced and more demanding format. Prerequisites for 9th Grade Honors English include the recommendation from the 8th grade Language Arts teacher, successful completion of the 8th grade Language Arts curriculum with a grade of B or better, BFUHS English department approval as well as successful completion of the summer reading/writing assignments.

courses.description: English 10 Enrichment is a semester-long course through which students work to develop and demonstrate mastery of the PBGR proficiencies associated with 10th Grade English. Students work to build their reading, writing, and communication skills to gain the background they will need for completion of elective classes during their junior and senior years. Fluency instruction is an important element of the class which students participate in daily to increase smooth reading and to develop reading speed. Students also work to develop writing skills while following the regular English 10 curriculum which includes poetry, public speaking and drama as well. *Students cannot self- enroll into this course; enrollment is based on team recommendation.

The sophomore English program, which covers four areas (Poetry, Drama, Writing and Speech,) is designed to develop important analysis and communication skills and give students additional background needed for completion of elective courses during their junior and senior years. Through the work completed in this course, students will develop their expository writing skills, broaden their understanding of drama as a literary form, work to understand the topics and techniques in poetry, and study speech, theory, and style. This course instructs and assesses a number of the Common Core Standards which students work to master throughout their high school careers. * The 10th Grade Honors English course covers the same areas of study but in a faster paced and more demanding format. Prerequisites for 10th Grade Honors English include a recommendation from the English Department (especially the 9th grade English teacher), successful completion of the 9th grade program with a grade of B or better and successful completion of the summer reading/writing assignments.

courses.description: This course provides intensive reading and writing which offers students a wide variety of literature to respond to and reflect on the actions we make as individuals and how this affects our natural environment, and our local, national, and global communities. Course literature will engage in a focused study of works written over the last several decades representative of different genres, and students will critically examine the impact culture and society have had on these authors and the impact writers have had on their audiences.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of the 9th and 10th grade English classes are a requirement for these classes.

courses.description: The American Studies course covers the American Experience from colonization to the present. Through the study of history, literature, art, architecture, and music, students explore the economic, cultural, and historical forces shaping America and its people. Students are afforded opportunities to develop critical thinking skills through reading primary documents and representative literature, responding in various forms of writing, and participating in relevant discussions. This is taught by a two-member team from the Social Studies Department and the English Department. This course bears one English and one United States History credit. To receive level 4 credit in American Studies students will be required to read an additional book each quarter and complete a 5-7 page essay through which they analyze the historical accuracy of the literature.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of the 9th and 10th grade English standards.
courses.fulfills_text: This course bears one English and one United States History credit.
courses.notes: Level 3; Also listed in Social Studies (p. 18), where it is described as co-taught by an English teacher and a social studies teacher; counts toward the U.S. History requirement

courses.description: Students who want to be able to express themselves confidently in front of an audience would benefit from this course. In this course students will use the techniques of dramatic performance to find their voice and improve oral and written communication. This will involve both creative writing and the performance of dramatic monologues, scenes, poetry and fiction. No acting experience is necessary. This course may also be taken as an elective credit.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of the 9th and 10th grade English classes are a requirement for these classes.

courses.description: Using a variety of digital mediums, students will focus on developing critical thinking skills that will aid them in not only interpreting/deciphering the complex media world of today, but also allow them to add to and actively participate in it as well. Students will examine a wide array of media content and develop an understanding of how the language and style the media uses, impacts the world we live in. Areas of study include advertising, censorship, media ethics, internet safety and living in the digital age.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of the 9th and 10th grade English classes are a requirement for these classes.

courses.description: In this writing intensive course, students study and focus on the essay and research paper using 21st-century skills. While the focus of the course is academic writing, students will engage in diverse activities outside the realm of traditional “papers.” Students will focus on using digital tools, the Internet, and web 2.0 tools to help them research, organize, evaluate, and communicate information. Using various forms of technology becomes the focus for exploring, reading and writing several types of essays and the research paper.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of the 9th and 10th grade English classes are a requirement for these classes.
courses.notes: Level 3; Dual Enrollment Course (course is available for CCV College Credit.)

courses.description: This course is a general survey of American writers, literary trends, and major movements in the development of our national literature. It provides a foundation for the study of American Literature with relatively challenging work beginning with the emerging literature of America, through the twentieth century. This course is unique in that it will cover literature by writers of the time along with a contemporary companion to explore themes. Through readings, lectures, and discussions, the semester is spent familiarizing the student with the rich literature of America and developing the ability to analyze literature critically.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation as well as successful completion of a quality summer reading/ writing assignment.
courses.notes: Level 4; Dual Enrollment Course (course is available for CCV College Credit.)

courses.description: In this course students survey the literature from England, Wales, Ireland and the British Empire, including in-depth studies of Chaucer, Shakespeare, Charles Dickens, and James Joyce. Films will provide cultural and historical background. This is a literature course designed for college bound juniors and seniors who wish to develop their skills in writing essays, reading and analyzing literature.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation as well as successful completion of a quality summer reading/ writing assignment.

courses.description: Designed to challenge our most capable and motivated seniors, A.P. English resembles the freshman English courses taught in many colleges. It requires extensive reading, writing, and discussion while preparing students for the rigors of a college English class and for the A.P. English Exam. In its approach to reading, the course involves students in the experience, interpretation, and evaluation of literature representing a wide range of genres and literary periods. Writing, another integral part of the course, will focus on critical analysis, including expository, analytical, and argumentative essays, but creative writing opportunities will also be provided. Additionally, language and literary theory will be introduced. Students should expect to read approximately twenty full-length works and write, on average, a significant paper every two weeks during the semester.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation as well as successful completion of the quality summer reading/ writing assignments.

courses.description: In this course, students will be challenged to consider what responsibility they have – within their political, social and local spheres – to participate as active global citizens. Students will learn to identify bias and think critically about diversity, equity, and inclusion. Students will explore public policy as well as ideologies and norms embedded in institutions and American society at large. Topics will include civic engagement, media literacy, race, gender, sexuality, class, and popular culture among others. At the end of this course, students will be better able to analyze evidence in order to construct their own critical opinions about ideas and practices in our society and in their own lives. They will have learned skills in order to become active global citizens.
courses.fulfills_text: one (1) required credit in modern world studies

courses.description: This is a one semester class that will fulfill the mandatory modern World History credit for graduation. The United Nations defined the concept of sustainability in 1987 as “meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.” We are all interconnected and decisions made at the local level can have global impact and vice versa. In this class, we will learn about the concept of sustainability, the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, and then apply the goals to current world issue case studies. Completing this course successfully will give you a strong foundation in current issues around the world and the efforts being made to manage those problems through the lens of sustainability.
courses.fulfills_text: will fulfill the mandatory modern World History credit for graduation

courses.notes: Level 4; Credits not printed for this entry (listed with 228 Seeking Sustainability, 1 credit)

courses.description: This course will examine the non-western world with students being introduced to the various regions and countries of the world. The role of culture, history and government in current world affairs will be explored. Regional issues will be examined in the context of globalization, economics, human rights and sustainability. This course concentrates on the modern world from the 20th century to today.
courses.fulfills_text: one (1) required credit in modern world studies

courses.description: This course will look at modern World History, starting with the early modern period of the Renaissance and going up to the early 21st century and today. Students will develop an understanding of world history, seeing how geography, religion, economics, government, and culture affect development. Current events and current issues will also be explored. Students will learn about different ways of looking at world issues, analyzing and comparing different world views and perspectives.
courses.fulfills_text: one (1) required credit in modern world studies

courses.description: This Advanced Placement (AP) course is taught to prepare students for the AP World History Exam in May. A high score on the exam may earn students college credit. The focus of the course is on themes, outlined by the College Board. This Advanced Placement course presents a very detailed account of history. It covers the history of the world, dealing with prehistory up until the present (but a large portion is based more in modern history). Throughout the study of history, we will examine the political, social, and economic changes between civilizations. We will also analyze the effects that religions, governments, and ideals had on the world throughout history. The course is set up through various periods throughout history. The course also focuses on nine historical thinking skills for reading and writing in history.
courses.prerequisites: Upon successful completion of a teacher-determined summer reading and writing assignment, students will demonstrate the ability to read and write at an Advanced Placement level and be able to understand specific course-related concepts that will be covered on the first day of class and throughout the course. Prior to the beginning of this course, a student must also meet with the teacher to review course expectations.
courses.fulfills_text: one (1) required credit in modern world studies

courses.description: Overview of U.S. History is a one semester class that will fulfill the mandatory U.S. History credit for graduation. The class will focus on the development of America from the Civil War until the end of the 20th Century and will examine the social, political, and economic issues America faced as well as the impact those events have had on the development of the American Society. In order to gain a greater understanding of the history of America, students will be required to examine a variety of sources including primary sources. Students will also be asked to interpret historical data and examine graphs and charts in order to understand the developments within the American political and economic system. Students will be required to do a variety of writing including works of historical fiction, research papers, editorials and letters throughout class.
courses.fulfills_text: will fulfill the mandatory U.S. History credit for graduation

courses.description: This Advanced Placement (AP) course is taught to prepare students for the AP United States History Exam in May. A high score on the exam may earn students college credit. This course will be taught at the college level and there will be a heavy emphasis on enhancing reading comprehension and promoting effective written communication. Class members will be expected to make use of primary sources to help them view American History from a variety of perspectives. Students will engage in a variety of activities that will help further their understanding of the people, places and events that shaped American History.
courses.prerequisites: Upon successful completion of a teacher-determined summer reading and writing assignment, students will demonstrate the ability to read and write at an Advanced Placement level and be able to understand specific course-related concepts that will be covered on the first day of class and throughout the course. Prior to the beginning of this course, a student must also meet with the teacher to review course expectations.
courses.fulfills_text: one (1) required credit in U.S. History

courses.description: This course will deal with psychological and sociological theory and research. Students will be exposed to a variety of viewpoints as they develop their own perspectives on relevant issues. The class is largely discussion-based. The course focuses on the impact that social forces have on individuals and society. It also analyzes the impact that genetics and the environment have on behavior. The course centers on various significant influences on individuals such as motivation, levels of consciousness, learning, and psychological disorders. At times, sensitive topics will be discussed, and students need to be prepared for that.

This course is designed to give students an understanding of the basic principles of economics. It will include micro/macroeconomics, a comparison of economic systems and world equity markets, and an introduction to theory and relevant terminology. A major focus will be an examination of the implications of globalization.

The goal of this course is to understand and comprehend the major events of the 20th century through the medium of film. This semester-long course will examine the major events of the world throughout the 20th century, from the colonization and independence movements of the early 1900’s through the Cold War, to current global issues. Students will be expected to participate in class discussions, read primary and secondary source documents, research topics independently, and write several in-depth essays over the events we will discuss. Religion, economics, government, politics, geography, ethnicity, and philosophy are just a few areas of the social studies curriculum that we will utilize and explore to aid in our discussion of major events. The medium of film will be used to generate discussion and increase comprehension and understanding of these events and their impact on the world we live in today.
courses.fulfills_text: one (1) required credit in modern world studies

courses.description: This Advanced Placement (AP) course is taught to prepare students for the AP Comparative Government and Politics Exam in May. A high score on the exam may earn students college credit. AP Comparative Government and Politics introduces students to the rich diversity of political life outside the United States. The course uses a comparative approach to examine the political structures; policies; and the political, economic, and social challenges among six selected countries: Great Britain, Mexico, Russia, Iran, China, and Nigeria. Additionally, students examine how different governments solve similar problems by comparing the effectiveness of approaches to many global issues.
courses.prerequisites: Upon successful completion of a teacher-determined summer reading and writing assignment, students will demonstrate the ability to read a college level textbook and write grammatically correct, complete sentences. Prior to the beginning of this course, a student must also meet with the teacher to review course expectations.

courses.description: This semester-long course is designed to provide students with an intense focus on current events that may not be covered in any other Social Studies courses. Topics vary based on student and teacher interest, but are mainly focused on controversial social and political issues. There is a focus on government and constitutional law to help interpret the legal status of each issue. A major component of the course is the development of critical thinking skills, bias identification and collecting reliable evidence to support opinions in regards to controversial topics as well as discussing and debating these topics intelligently while respecting other points of view.

¡Bienvenidos al mundo de español! Welcome to the world of Spanish! In Spanish I will introduce the student to the Spanish-speaking world: the people, their culture and customs. Students will learn the pronunciation and basic grammatical structures of Spanish while also building vocabulary, and the comprehension of conversational Spanish by using storytelling. The stories are an essential part of our class, and they are both students produced as a class, but also introduced throughout each unit. These stories do not isolate grammatical topics, and are used to build grammatical and vocabulary foundations and overall confidence for students. Students will increase their understanding of the language and their ability to communicate through a variety of learning activities and materials, including videos, music and songs, role-plays, current events and news, computer programs and the Internet, and artistic expression.

¡Tú hablas español! You speak Spanish! In Spanish II emphasis will be placed on continued development of the basic conversational skills, as well as expanding appreciation of the Hispanic culture. Students will continue to improve their Spanish primarily through the use of storytelling. Once again, as in Spanish One, these stories do not isolate grammatical topics, and are used to build grammatical and vocabulary foundations and overall confidence for students.Students will continue to work with higher level grammatical structures and vocabulary through the various learning activities and materials used in Spanish I.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation, proficiency in Spanish I language skills.

courses.description: ¡Trabajamos más en español! Let’s work more in Spanish! Intermediate Spanish III marks the first steps in intermediate language study. Students will have mastered basic communication skills and grammatical structures and are ready to move into more complex areas of the language. Students will continue to improve their Spanish primarily through the use of storytelling. Once again, as in Spanish One & Two, these stories do not isolate grammatical topics, and are used to build grammatical and vocabulary foundations and overall confidence for students. Confidence in speaking will be supported through student-led discussions and role plays. Reading and writing will become more of a focus, along with continued emphasis on speaking and listening. Projects and presentations will offer the students interesting avenues for expression, as well as opportunities for doing research.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation and proficiency in language skills appropriate for this level.

courses.description: The first half of a more concrete approach to the same topics covered in Algebra I. This course is designed for the students who have mastered most of Vermont’s 8th grade standards but not all. Between this course and the follow-up course of Algebra I part II, students will be introduced to the structure and properties of a mathematical system, including the basic operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division of signed numbers, algebraic expressions, solutions of equations and inequalities, and graphing. This course will include abstract mathematical topics and practical applications of the problem solving skills developed through Algebra.
courses.notes: Level 3; PBGRs: 1. Expressions, Equations, and Functions, 2. Linear Equations, 3. Linear Functions, 4. Equations of Linear Functions, 5. Linear Inequalities, 6. Systems of Linear Equations and Inequalities

courses.description: This course is the follow up course to Algebra I Part I. It will continue to cover Algebraic topics where the first course left off, continuing to use a concrete, practical approach. Successful completion of this course along with Algebra I Part I will meet the BFUHS Algebra graduation requirement and will sufficiently prepare the student for more advanced math courses.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with successful completion of Algebra I part I.
courses.fulfills_text: Successful completion of this course along with Algebra I Part I will meet the BFUHS Algebra graduation requirement
courses.notes: Level 3; PBGRs: 7. Exponents and Exponential Functions, 8. Quadratic Expressions on Equations, 9. Quadratic Functions and Equations, 10. Radical Functions and Geometry, 11. Rational Functions and Equations, 12. Statistics and Probability

courses.description: This fast paced course is for students who have mastered Vermont’s 8th grade standards, have strong reading ability, have interest and motivation in things mathematical and scientific and are willing to work in a rigorous college preparatory course. Students are introduced to the structure and properties of a mathematical system, including the basic operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division of signed numbers, algebraic expressions, solutions of equations and inequalities and graphing. Algebra I is an entry-level course for college-bound students that meets for one semester. No longer offered the 2022-2023 School year.

courses.description: Part I will cover basic elements of geometry, proofs, parallel and perpendicular lines, the coordinate plane, triangles, quadrilaterals and transformations.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of Algebra I, parts I & 2. A scientific calculator is recommended.
courses.notes: Level 3; PBGRs: 1. Tools of Geometry, 2. Proofs, 3. Parallel and Perpendicular Lines, 4. Congruent Triangles, 5. Relationships in Triangles, 6. Quadrilaterals, 9. Transformations

courses.description: Part II will first finish the regular Geometry curriculum: circles, trigonometry, congruence and similarity, surface area, and volume. Scientific and/or graphing calculators will be used extensively and one or the other is required. If a student plans to take Algebra II, the department recommends a graphing calculator now. If a student does not plan to take Algebra II, then a scientific calculator will suffice. Students may check with the department coordinator in the spring or the teacher at the start of the class to find out which brand of calculator is recommended.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of Geometry, Part 1. A scientific calculator is required.
courses.notes: Level 3; PBGRs: 7. Proportions and Similarity, 8. Right Triangles and Trigonometry, 10. Circles, 11. Area, Surface Area, Lateral Area, and Volume, 12. Probability

courses.description: This is an extremely rigorous, fast-paced course. Fast paced Geometry is a comprehensive look at the study of geometric concepts of Geometry Parts 1 & 2, including the basic elements of geometry, proofs, parallel and perpendicular lines, the coordinate plane, triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, circles, trigonometry, congruence and similarity, surface area, volume and transformations. This course meets in one semester.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of Alg I. A scientific calculator is required.
courses.notes: Level 3.5; PBGRs: 1. Tools of Geometry, 2. Proofs, 3. Parallel and Perpendicular Lines, 4. Congruent Triangles, 5. Relationships in Triangles, 6. Quadrilaterals, 7. Proportions and Similarity, 8. Right Triangles and Trigonometry, 9. Transformations, 10. Circles, 11. Area, Surface Area, Lateral Area, and Volume, 12. Probability

courses.description: All topics and PBGRs covered in Honors Algebra II (see page 30) will be covered in this course and Algebra II part II. Additionally, students will study these topics: exponential and logarithmic functions, conic sections, sequences and series, probability, as well as SAT review.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of Algebra I A graphing calculator is required. Staff recommends one of the following: TI-84, TI-84 Plus CE.
courses.notes: Level 3; PBGRs: 1. Linear Equations, 2. Relations and Functions, 3. Quadratic Functions, 4. Polynomials and Polynomial Functions, 5. Inverses and Radical Functions 6. Matrices (time permitting)

courses.description: All topics and PBGRs covered in Honors Algebra II will be covered in this course (and Algebra II Part I). Additionally, students will study these topics: exponential and logarithmic functions, conic sections, sequences and series, probability, as well as SAT review.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of Algebra II Part I. A graphing calculator is required. Staff recommends one of the following: TI-84, TI-84 Plus CE.
courses.notes: Level 4; PBGRs: 6. Exponential and Logarithmic Functions, 7. Rational Functions, 8. Statistics and Probability, 9. Trigonometric Functions, 10. Trigonometric Identities and Equations

courses.description: This is an extremely rigorous, fast-paced semester course. It is a study of the structure of the real and complex numbers. The course is a continuation and elaboration of the ideas introduced in Algebra I, but is more abstract. Topics: linear equations and inequalities, the system of equations, and the solution of verbal problems. Concepts of functions and relations are examined. Graphing calculators will be used extensively and are required regularly for homework. *Successful completion of part 1 material and gaps in part 2 material may lead to a part 1 credit and the need to take part 2.
courses.prerequisites: B or better in Algebra I and teacher recommendation. A graphing calculator is required. Staff recommends one of the following: TI-84, TI-84 Plus CE .
courses.notes: Level 4; PBGRs: 1. Linear Equations, 2. Relations and Functions, 3. Quadratic Functions, 4. Polynomials and Polynomial Functions, 5. Inverses and Radical Functions, 6. Exponential and Logarithmic Functions, 7. Rational Functions, 8. Statistics and Probability, 9. Trigonometric Functions, 10. Trigonometric Identities and Equations

courses.description: The semester-long financial literacy course for Juniors and Seniors covers all of the essential personal finance topics necessary to become a financially capable young adult: budgeting, saving, banking, credit management, home/auto/college financing, insurance, taxation, retirement planning, investing and more. By the end of this course students will develop a better understanding of personal finance topics and be more prepared to handle their personal financial responsibilities as young adults.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra 1 and Geometry Part I. A scientific calculator and laptop for spreadsheet work will be required for this course.

courses.description: This course will introduce students to statistics, probability models, statistical estimation, hypothesis testing, linear regression analysis, and special topics. Statistics acquaints students with the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with the successful completion of Algebra II. A graphing calculator is required. Staff recommends one of the following: TI-84, TI-84 Plus CE.
courses.notes: Level 4; PBGRs 1. Exploring data: describing patterns and departures from patterns. 2. Sampling and experimentation:planning and conducting a study 3. Anticipating patterns:exploring random phenomena using probability and simulations. 4. Statistical Inference: estimating population parameters and testing hypothesis

courses.description: An advanced math course for students with a strong mathematical background. Topics covered will include functions and functional analysis, trigonometry, and advanced problem solving techniques. Graphing calculators will be used extensively and are required regularly for homework.
courses.prerequisites: A very strong understanding of the skills associated with success in Geometry and Algebra II. A graphing calculator is required. Staff recommends one of the following: TI-84, TI-84 Plus CE .
courses.notes: Level 4; PBGRs: 1. Functions from a Calculus Perspective, 2. Exponential and Logarithmic Functions, 3. Trigonometric Functions, 4. Trigonometric Identities and Equations, 5. Conic sections and Parametric Equations

courses.description: Open to highly motivated students with strong mathematical backgrounds and excellent reading skills. This course will run simultaneously with AP Calculus for one semester. All topics will be taught to both groups at the same depth, except the Honors curriculum will omit the topics of Related Rates or Optimizations. The Honors assessments will be similar to the AP assessments. Homework assignments will be identical, except that Honors curriculum will omit the AP test practice questions.
courses.prerequisites: The skills associated with successful completion of Pre-Calculus. A graphing calculator is required. Staff recommends one of the following: TI-84, TI-84 Plus CE .
courses.notes: Level 4; PBGRs: 1. Functions and Graphs 2. Derivative Functions 3. The Definite Integral 4. Differentiation Rules 5. Applications of the Derivative 6. Integrals 7. Finding Antiderivatives

courses.description: Open to highly motivated students with strong mathematical backgrounds and excellent reading skills. College-level work is expected and assignments are of that caliber. Students are required to take the Advanced Placement Calculus AP examination in May, therefore, the curriculum is that which is dictated by The College Board. A student who completes the course with a good grade may consider it the equivalent of a year of college calculus. Graphing calculators are required for the AP test and are therefore required for the course. The course will meet for a full block for the first half of the year and then meet for ½ block in the spring semester.
courses.prerequisites: A very strong understanding of the skills associated with successful completion of Pre-Calculus. A graphing calculator is required. Staff recommends one of the following: TI-84, TI-84 Plus CE.
courses.notes: Level 5; PBGRs: 1. Functions and Graphs 2. Derivative Functions 3. The Definite Integral 4. Differentiation Rules 5. Applications of the Derivative 6. Integrals 7. Finding Antiderivatives 8. Using the Definite Integral (including volumes of solids by revolution and cross-section) 9. Differential Equations 10. Slope Fields 11. L’Hopital’s Rule; Dual Enrollment Course (course is available for RVCC College Credit.)

courses.description: This course is designed for freshmen. Earth Science is the study of the earth's origins, structure, and processes. It draws upon each of the three main branches of science: Physics, Chemistry, and Biology. Earth Science includes, but is not limited to: hydrology, geography, meteorology, geology, and astronomy. The course will give an introduction to the methods of science and an overview of basic physical science concepts. Topics covered include but are not limited to plate tectonics, watershed science, global climate, and the sun-earth-moon system. Students will understand and analyze the origins, interactions and relationships between and among the Earth, our solar system, and the universe as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (ESS1). Students will also understand and analyze Earth’s systems and the relationship between human activity and the earth as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (ESS2 & ESS3). The foundation level course will cover the same basic materials as the level 3 version, however it will allow for additional time on material, more hands-on instruction, and additional support throughout the class. It will also spend additional time building up the science basics before diving into specific material. Students should successfully complete Earth Science/Honors Earth Science before taking other science classes.

This course is designed for freshmen. Earth Science is the study of the earth's origins, structure, and processes. It draws upon each of the three main branches of science: Physics, Chemistry, and Biology. Earth Science includes, but is not limited to: hydrology, geography, meteorology, geology, and astronomy. The course will give an introduction to the methods of science and an overview of basic physical science concepts. Topics covered include plate tectonics, watershed science, global climate, and the sun-earth-moon system. Students will understand and analyze the origins, interactions and relationships between and among the Earth, our solar system, and the universe as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (ESS1). Students will also understand and analyze Earth’s systems and the relationship between human activity and the earth as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (ESS2 & ESS3). Students should successfully complete Earth Science/Honors Earth Science before taking other science classes.

This course is designed for freshmen with solid academic skills in reading, writing, and mathematics, a strong interest in learning science, and excellent study habits. Earth Science is the study of the Earth's origins, structure, and processes. It draws upon each of the three main branches of science: Physics, Chemistry, and Biology. Earth science includes, but is not limited to: hydrology, geography, meteorology, geology, and astronomy. The course will give an introduction to the methods of science and an overview of basic physical science concepts. Topics covered include plate tectonics, watershed science, global climate, and the sun-earth-moon system. Students will understand and analyze the origins, interactions and relationships between and among the Earth, our solar system, and the universe as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (ESS1). Students will also understand and analyze Earth’s systems and the relationship between human activity and the earth as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (ESS2 & ESS3). Students must successfully complete Earth Science/Honors Earth Science before taking other science classes.

This course is designed for sophomores. Emphasis is placed on basic biology subject matter including ecology, the cell, evolution, genetics, energy, and ecology. The foundation level course will cover the same basic materials as the level 3 version, however it will allow for additional time on material, more hands-on instruction, and additional support throughout the class. It will also spend additional time building up the science basics before diving into specific material. Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas: 1. Understand and analyze molecular, structural, and chemical biology as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 1); 2. Understand and analyze the characteristics, functions, and behavioral interactions within an ecosystem as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 2); and, 3. Understand and analyze genetics, adaptation, and biodiversity as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 3 + LS 4).
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science

courses.description: This course is designed for sophomores. Emphasis is placed on basic biology subject matter including ecology, the cell, evolution, genetics, energy, and taxonomy. It is a fast-paced, active, hands-on class with high expectations for students. Completion of this class with a B or better will prepare for upper level electives and for the college experience. Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas: 1. Understand and analyze molecular, structural, and chemical biology as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 1); 2. Understand and analyze the characteristics, functions, and behavioral interactions within an ecosystem as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 2); and, 3. Understand and analyze genetics, adaptation, and biodiversity as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 3 + LS 4).
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science.

courses.description: This course is designed for high-achieving, college-bound students who may intend to pursue further studies in the life science and related fields and who would like a substantial amount of laboratory experience for college entrance. Emphasis is placed on an extension of basic subject matter (including the cell, genetics, evolution, human physiology, and basic ecology) to include inductive reasoning skills and open-ended lab investigations. Students should have strong written and oral communication skills and strong math skills. Written lab reports, daily homework assignments, frequent tests and quizzes, research papers and other projects will be required. This course is generally taken after Honors Earth Science. Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas: 1. Understand and analyze molecular, structural, and chemical biology as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS1); 2. Understand and analyze the characteristics, functions, and behavioral interactions within an ecosystem as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS2); and, 3. Understand and analyze genetics, adaptation, and biodiversity as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS3 & LS4). Students in the honors level course are expected to exceed the standard level of proficiency for the indicators of this course.
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science.

courses.description: This course presents a challenging introduction to chemistry. Lectures, readings, laboratory investigations and problem solving provide insight into the chemical properties of matter and the causes and effects of chemical interactions. Topics include: atomic structure, chemical reactivity, energy and entropy, equilibrium, kinetics, acid-base, oxidation-reduction and electrochemistry. Problem solving and critical thinking skills will be developed and applied. High expectations for student effort and performance make this course appropriate for college or career oriented students. Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas. Students will be able to understand and analyze matter, reactions and physical systems as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (PS 1 & PS 2). Students will use the periodic table as a model to predict the relative properties of elements based on the patterns of electrons in the outermost energy level of atoms. (HS-PS1-1), construct and revise an explanation for the outcome of a simple chemical reaction based on the outermost electron state of atoms, trends in the periodic table, and knowledge of the patterns of chemical properties. (HS-PS1-2), plan and conduct an investigation to gather evidence to compare the structure of substances at the bulk scale to infer the strength of electrical forces between particles. (HS-PS1-3), and develop a model to illustrate that the release or absorption of energy from a chemical reaction system depends upon the changes in total bond energy. (HS-PS1-4).
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology, and Algebra I (or be concurrently enrolled in Algebra I or higher.)

courses.description: Chemistry is the study of matter, its structure, properties and composition, and the changes that matter undergoes. A major goal is to develop a new way of looking at things, problem solving and critical thinking skills. The course is meant to be challenging and teacher expectations of the student are high. Laboratory work is used to discover the nature of matter and develop chemical laboratory skills. The students will discover that algebra is part of the language of chemistry. Topical content is similar to that of General Chemistry. However, there is a greater emphasis on quantitative problem solving and application of chemical principles. This course is designed for college-bound students with a good background in mathematics, who intend to pursue a scientific or health-care focused course of study. Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas. Students will be able to understand and analyze matter, reactions and physical systems as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (PS 1 & PS 2). Students will use the periodic table as a model to predict the relative properties of elements based on the patterns of electrons in the outermost energy level of atoms. (HS-PS1-1), construct and revise an explanation for the outcome of a simple chemical reaction based on the outermost electron state of atoms, trends in the periodic table, and knowledge of the patterns of chemical properties. (HS-PS1-2), plan and conduct an investigation to gather evidence to compare the structure of substances at the bulk scale to infer the strength of electrical forces between particles. (HS-PS1-3), and develop a model to illustrate that the release or absorption of energy from a chemical reaction system depends upon the changes in total bond energy. (HS-PS1-4). Students in the honors level course are expected to exceed the standard level of proficiency for the indicators of this course.
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science, and Biology/Honors Biology and Algebra I or higher.

courses.description: Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas. Students will be able to (1) understand and analyze energy and the characteristics and dynamics of waves as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (PS 3 & PS 4), (2) Plan an investigation to provide evidence that the change in an object’s motion depends on the mass of the object. (MS-PS2-2), (3) Ask questions about data to determine the factors that affect the strength of electric and magnetic forces.(MS-PS2-3), (4) Construct and present arguments using evidence to support the claim that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on the masses of interacting objects (MS-PS2-4), and (4) Conduct an investigation and evaluate the experimental design to provide evidence that fields exist between objects exerting forces on each other even though the objects are not in contact. (MS-PS2-5).
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology, and Algebra I or higher.

courses.description: Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas. Students will be able to (1) understand and analyze energy and the characteristics and dynamics of waves as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (PS 3 + PS 4), (2) Plan an investigation to provide evidence that the change in an object’s motion depends on the mass of the object. (MS-PS2-2), (3) Ask questions about data to determine the factors that affect the strength of electric and magnetic forces.(MS-PS2-3), (4) Construct and present arguments using evidence to support the claim that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on the masses of interacting objects. (MS-PS2-4), and (5) Conduct an investigation and evaluate the experimental design to provide evidence that fields exist between objects exerting forces on each other even though the objects are not in contact. (MS-PS2-5). Students in the honors level course are expected to exceed the standard level of proficiency for the indicators of this course.
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology, and Algebra I and concurrent enrollment in Algebra II or higher.

courses.description: Forensic Science is the application of science to those criminal and civil laws that are enforced by police agencies in a criminal justice system. It has become a comprehensive subject incorporating Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Entomology, Earth Science, Anatomy and Physiology as well as other aspects of Science. Major topics include processing a crime scene, collecting and preserving evidence, identifying types of physical evidence, organic and inorganic analysis of evidence, hair, fibers, and paint, toxicology, arson and explosion investigations, serology, DNA, fingerprints, firearms, and document analysis . The main focus of this course will be to emphasize the evidential value of crime scene and related evidence and the services of what has become known as the crime laboratory. This course combines basic theory and real laboratory experiments, using a case-study based situation for the better understanding of the students. The experiments used reinforce previously learned scientific principles rooted in Biology, Chemistry and Physics. (LS1-4, PS1-4)
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology

courses.description: This 1 credit course is designed for juniors and seniors who have a special interest in ocean science and marine biology. This class will only be available in the fall semester. We will investigate ocean systems and compare a variety of saltwater ecosystems to our local freshwater ecosystems (HS-LS2-4+LS2-5). Students will conduct water quality tests and learn how organisms in both habitats are specifically adapted to their environment. (HS-ESS2-4+Ess2-5) Students will grow to appreciate the biodiversity of aquatic species found in oceanic and freshwater ecosystems, and will learn that to preserve healthy aquatic ecosystems is to sustain a healthy quality of life for all. We may have a field trip opportunity to the University of New Hampshire Floating Lab program. If possible, students will board a whale watching boat equipped with scientific equipment and conduct laboratory testing of the Gulf of Maine. https://seagrant.unh.edu/coastal-floating-lab (LS2A-C, LS1A)
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology.
courses.offering_note: Class is only available in Fall semester

courses.description: This course is designed for juniors and seniors with a solid interest in space. Students must have successfully completed Earth Science and Biology. This course will provide an in-depth study of the universe and technology utilized in studying objects in space. The course will draw upon Physics and Earth Science to develop an understanding of the laws that govern the universe.s. Topics covered include but are not limited to: planetology, cosmology, exploration of space (technology used in exploration), solar systems, deep space objects, and the search for life. Students are expected to take an active role during class time. This class has a blending of lecture and student research. Students will be expected to do research and teach their peers about what they learn.. Besides classroom work, students will complete an observational component as well as a research paper. (ESS1)
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology

courses.description: This course is designed for juniors and seniors who have completed earth science and biology. This course will focus on the many natural disasters humankind may face. From meteorological events such as tornadoes and hurricanes, to geological events like earthquakes, volcanoes, and landslides, the main emphasis will be on how when these phenomena are better understood people have a better chance of minimizing the impacts. The focus will be on project based learning and labs alongside class discussions on the current topic being covered. Students will gain a better understanding of the destructive forces of nature while also gaining a new lens with which to view the world. (ESS2D, ESS3B, ESS3C, ESS3D)
courses.prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology

courses.description: This course is designed to give any singer study and experience in Choral music. A wide variety of choral literature will be rehearsed and performed. In addition, the technical aspects of singing, sight singing, and working as an ensemble, will be covered. All participants must perform at all performances scheduled by the Director.

Students in the courses will study a wide range of musical styles and perform music for concert band, marching band and pep band as well as solos and small ensembles. Students will receive regular individual and/or small group instruction in addition to the large ensemble rehearsals. Students are required to participate in all performances scheduled by the director. Band members are eligible to audition for District Music Festivals, as well as for the Vermont All-State Music Festival. This requires outside preparation on the part of the individual. This course is open to students able to demonstrate a strong foundation in basic literacy and performance skills on their musical instrument.

Students in this course will study and perform music from the jazz repertoire, including swing, blues, funk, and latin styles. Students will learn music theory and aural skills while developing the necessary improvisation skills central to the jazz tradition. This course is open to students able to demonstrate a strong foundation in basic literacy and performance skills on their musical instrument.

Students in this course will study and perform popular music from recent decades, including rock, pop, reggae, hip-hop, rhythm & blues, country, electronic dance music, and other emerging styles. Students will have the opportunity to study the guitar, bass, drums, and/or keyboard as well as vocals and music technology. This course is open to all students.

Students in this course will work collaboratively with the instructor to establish individualized learning goals and objectives. Students have the opportunity to begin learning a new instrument or further skills on a familiar instrument. Lessons are scheduled according to the student’s availability. This course is open to students at all levels.

This course is for students who are involved in the music program or are interested in becoming involved in the music program. The course work concentrates on technical skills, building a repertoire, and exploring an individual's potential. Lessons are scheduled according to a student's availability.

This class is for any student interested in theater arts and music, but also integrates visual art, dance and technical theater (set building and light and sound design). This class will primarily work on acting and vocal music skills, as well as introductions to basic dance and visual art for set design. It will additionally offer students the opportunity to train in technical theater through set design and building and light and sound design. Students will be trained on the necessary equipment to help them independently operate light and sound boards. Students will also be offered the student leadership opportunities to work on directing, choreography, vocal music peer assistance, as well as visual set design. This is a class for any student interested in either on or off stage roles in the world of musical theater!

This course is designed to teach students a deeper understanding of our musical language through rhythm, melody, harmony, form, and more.Throughout the course, students will explore the elements of music notation, including key signatures, time signatures, scales, and intervals. They will develop a strong foundation in understanding harmony and chord progressions, enabling them to analyze and interpret musical compositions across various genres. Additionally, the course will cover the historical context of music theory, allowing students to appreciate how musical conventions have evolved over time. Students will develop skills including sight-reading, ear training, and composition. By the end of the course, students will be able to not only read and analyze sheet music but also compose their own musical pieces, applying the principles learned throughout the curriculum. This Music Theory course encourages critical thinking and creative expression, fostering a deeper connection to the art of music. Whether students aspire to pursue further studies in music or simply wish to enhance their overall musical literacy, this course provides a solid foundation for a lifelong appreciation of the intricate language of music.

In this course, students will explore the cultural, historical, and musical background of American Popular Music. Course activities will explore cultural connections, how music reflects social & cultural awareness, and technological developments that impacted the evolution of popular music. Each unit will focus on a different genre musical, or decade, and contain four lessons based on the National Core Arts Standards of Creating, Presenting/Performing/Producing, Responding, and Connecting with variable tasks.

Art 1 is a foundation course open to all students at all levels. The primary focus in this class is on the foundations of drawing, painting, and basic composition. Using the Elements (color, line, shape, space, texture, value) and Principles of Design (balance, emphasis, proportion, rhythm, unity, and variety/contrast) to guide us, we will explore drawing media (pencil, colored pencils, charcoal, pen and ink, brush and ink) and acrylic paints. Experimentation with printmaking and non-traditional tools and media will be introduced. Basic art history and critical analysis will be addressed weekly. This is the perfect class to take to get your art credit, explore your inner artist and is a prerequisite for any of the advanced art classes/honors credit.
courses.fulfills_text: This is the perfect class to take to get your art credit

courses.description: This class is also a foundation course and is open to all students at all levels. This class will focus on using the Elements (color, line, shape, space, texture, value) and Principles of Design (balance, emphasis, proportion, rhythm, unity, and variety/contrast) to create sound compositions. Rather than using traditional art media, students will use their phone cameras, some digital cameras, and alternative photographic techniques, such as cyanotypes. Some very basic photo editing will expand student creative explorations. The willingness for experimentation is heartily encouraged. Basic photographic history and critical analysis will be addressed weekly. This class will meet your art credit requirements, but will not meet advanced art prerequisites.
courses.fulfills_text: This class will meet your art credit requirements, but will not meet advanced art prerequisites.

courses.description: This class builds on the foundations and fundamental skills introduced in Art 1. More traditional and non-traditional media will be explored. Sophisticated handling of the Elements and Principles of Design will be a primary focus. Portraiture and the human figure will be a major subject covered throughout this course. Painting techniques, (impasto, grisaille, alla prima, and scumbling) will be experimented with along with different types of water-based paint as students develop their own, personal aesthetics. Students will expand their basic skills and strategies as they develop related bodies of work. Art history and critical analysis will be at a more advanced level than Art 1 and will include some in-depth investigations of certain time periods and artists.
courses.prerequisites: Art 1

courses.description: This printmaking class introduces students to the basic materials, equipment and processes for the production of multiple images from a master plate. The printmaking processes that this class will explore include monotype, relief block, collagraph, and chine colle. Students will create plates out of a variety of materials and then “pull” images by hand or through the use of a hand-run printing press. Emphasis is on design and composition as well as creative use of the materials and techniques of the relief (wood block and linoleum block), monoprint, and serigraph (silkscreen and stencil) printing processes. Experimentation with different kinds of ink, ink application, and handmade paper will also be a focus. Students are expected to explore the role of the printmaker in society and the significance of prints as a vital form of communication. Additionally, the history of printmaking and associated critical analysis will be addressed regularly throughout the course. Honors credit will be given to students who have previously, and successfully completed Art 1 and complete additional assignments.

This introductory course will introduce students to pottery as an art form. Students will learn the basic handbuilding and decorative techniques to create original ceramic pieces. This work will range from traditional, functional ware to imaginative, sculptural forms. Surface decoration and manipulation as well as glazing and underglazing techniques will be covered fully. A variety of historical and contemporary work observed throughout the class for inspiration and appreciation. Students will also experience making pottery on the potter’s wheel. This class offers a creative experience with many challenges, discoveries and rewards. Classes will be limited to upperclassmen (juniors and seniors) with a class size limited to 14. Honors credit will be given to students who have previously, and successfully, completed Art 1 and complete additional assignments.

This course introduces the design and production of relief sculpture and sculpture-in-the round and aims to develop spatial literacy through various 3D design and construction techniques. Students will design and construct realistic and abstract sculptural forms using a variety of materials, tools and techniques. Methods include the additive, subtractive, modeling and casting processes. Students will examine, analyze, and interpret traditional and contemporary works of art and artifacts while their understanding of the elements and principles of design are reinforced. Students explore the structural, compositional and conceptual implications of commonly used materials, such as cardboard, wood, metal, plaster and found objects, and are instructed on the safe use of select hand and power tools. Sketchbook and minor research assignments are a part of this course. Honors credit will be given to students who have previously, and successfully, completed Art 1 and complete additional assignments.

Foods will consist of scaffolded learning from basic to advanced methods of food preparation. Students are responsible for maintaining kitchen safety and sanitation of kitchen areas. Students will work in teams to follow recipes as well as gain competence in creating recipes and menus specific to occasion, dietary restrictions, and lifestyle. Identifying interpersonal skills and character traits necessary for successful collaboration will be part of our daily practice. Kitchen labs will focus on cooking delicious food and social emotional learning will happen through opportunities to participate in community building games and reflective processing. Nutrition, wellness, and a basic understanding of how healthy eating relates to obesity and other preventable diseases is provided. Students will gain knowledge about lifestyle choices and ways to incorporate healthy habits.

International Foods is an elective course in Family & Consumer Sciences. It is strongly recommended that Foods class is taken prior to this class as the basics of kitchen prep knowledge are necessary for time management in the foods labs. Students explore and research the history of food and preparation as it relates to diverse cultures and International cuisines. Students will gain a better understanding of ingredients, agricultural methods, eating utensils, cooking methods and customs of the global society in which we live.

Using the framework of cooking competitions such as Chopped, Nailed it, Great British Baking Show, Iron Chef, cupcake wars, pie contest, chili cook-off, etc students will plan recipes and learn to hone their skills building up to competitions in a fun and exciting atmosphere.

In Decorative Touch, students will explore their unique creativity on an individual and collective basis. Students will learn about elements of design and have the opportunity to apply knowledge of design composition to create an assortment of hands-on projects including upcycling materials, sewing and textiles, preparing fancy appetizers, high end desserts, and cake decorating.
Creative and functional projects using fabric and textiles including sewing, stitching, embroidery, weaving, bleach painting and upcycling clothes.

Proficiencies for our Health courses are met through a combination of online and in-person workshops to align with State of Vermont requirements. The State of VT defines health literacy as “the capacity of students to obtain, interpret and understand basic health information and service, and the competence to use such information and services in ways that enhance health.” Health topics will include nutrition, interpersonal communication, mental health, healthy relationships, sexual health and substance use. As part of our focus on health, students will also review basic first aid and CPR. In addition to the online (.5 credit) requirement, students can fulfill the remaining .5 BFUHS health requirement through successful completion of related online or in-person courses, including Health Services programs at one of the Tech Centers.

All students are required to complete 1½ credits of Physical Education unless excused by a physician. We recommend that students get involved with P.E. all four years. Listed below are the activities offered in each season of the year. These activities are open to all students. - Fall: Flag Football, Conditioning, Fitness Testing, Frisbee Games, Hocker, Team Handball - Winter: Basketball, Weight Training, Volleyball, Badminton, Table Tennis, Floor Hockey, Pickleball, Snowshoeing and Orienteering - Spring: Softball and Wiffle Ball, Lacrosse, Tennis, Fitness Testing, Rec. Games All Physical Education classes spend about twenty minutes addressing physical wellness before moving to the regular activity unit of instruction. The components of physical fitness are addressed as follows: ● Cardio Respiratory Endurance: Students start by jogging three laps in the gym. One more lap is added each class meeting to build up to the one mile run. Everyone is encouraged to jog, but if unable to, they may walk. ● Agility is addressed by use of several footwork drills such as high knees, backwards running, slide steps or shuffle, and grapevine. ● Flexibility is addressed by several stretching activities. ● Muscular strength is addressed along with muscular endurance at the horizontal ladder, the chinning bar, and the weight room. ● Power is addressed by use of bounding drills or plyometrics. ● Body composition is addressed through the use of a body analyzer. ● Circuit training is also included as a physical wellness activity each quarter.
courses.fulfills_text: All students are required to complete 1½ credits of Physical Education unless excused by a physician.

courses.course_name: Traffic Safety Education (with a Vermont Certified Driver’s Education Program)
courses.description: Driver’s Education is intended to help develop / improve skills, knowledge, and confidence in the safe operation of motor vehicles. In order to sign up for a class in the community, you need to have a valid driver’s permit prior to the start of the course. A copy of your permit must be submitted to the Counseling Office. Once a copy of the permit has been submitted, a voucher request form will be provided to support payment on the student’s behalf to a Vermont certified private driver’s education program. For more information, please contact the Counseling Office.

The Title Math program provides students with supplemental instruction in math skills. Considering each student's uniqueness and special circumstances, the Title I teacher accommodates each student's own individual learning style by providing developmental instructional materials and innovative strategies that will enhance learning and enable the students to succeed in the regular academic program. Additionally, the program's teacher encourages and facilitates parent participation in their child's education.

This course provides students with supplemental support in reading and writing. This program affords its participants opportunities to practice skills necessary and appropriate for their grade and ability level. Considering each student’s uniqueness, the teacher works to accommodate a student’s individual learning style. Strategies are introduced to enhance learning and enable students to succeed in their scheduled classes.

This course focuses on and reinforces mastery of the skills required for facing a rigorous and demanding academic life in high school teaching/ reinforcing effective organization skills and positive study habits. Students will work with different reading and writing strategies to prepare them for the demands of courses at BFUHS. As well as academics, the course will prepare students to be successful in the 21st Century job market.

An Independent Study is an opportunity for students to pursue an advanced academic class in an area of interest. The student will need to find an appropriate staff member and a curriculum plan will need to be developed. It is the student’s responsibility to obtain and complete the appropriate Independent Study forms (from the school counseling office) prior to beginning the coursework. Students may earn no more than 1 credit per academic year via Independent Study.
courses.notes: Level - varies; program; also described under Flexible Pathways (Independent Studies, p. 5)

courses.description: Tier two and three level small group, supported study hall where students receive help in content area course work with an emphasis on reading, writing, and math for their work in their core academic classes as designated in the IEP. Students will learn a variety of strategies for active reading, note-taking, long-term project planning, test taking, test anxiety, and organizing material.
courses.prerequisites: Must be specified in the Individualized Education Plan.

courses.description: Tier two and three level small group, supported study hall where students receive help in content area course work with an emphasis on reading, writing, and math for their work in their core academic classes as designated in the IEP. Students will learn proactive approaches to self-advocacy and establish short and long-term goals related to promoting effective self-management. Research into options for post-secondary education and employment will also be addressed.
courses.prerequisites: Must be specified in the Individualized Education Plan.

courses.description: Students in tier two level English classes work on applying basic reading and writing skills that are approaching grade level. The intent of this class is to transition students into general education English classes. This course provides group and individual instruction according to a student’s IEP goals. This course provides alternative credit towards meeting the graduation requirement in English for students who have a learning disability that impacts reading and writing performance which cannot be accommodated in the general education setting.
courses.prerequisites: Must be specified in the Individualized Education Plan.
courses.fulfills_text: This course provides alternative credit towards meeting the graduation requirement in English for students who have a learning disability that impacts reading and writing performance which cannot be accommodated in the general education setting.

courses.description: Tier two level math classes work on pre-algebra and algebra skills with the intent to transition into general education math classes. This course provides group and individual instruction according to a student’s IEP goals. This course provides alternative credit towards meeting the graduation requirement in mathematics for students who have a learning disability that impacts math performance which cannot be accommodated in the general education setting.
courses.prerequisites: Must be specified in the Individualized Education Plan.
courses.fulfills_text: This course provides alternative credit towards meeting the graduation requirement in mathematics for students who have a learning disability that impacts math performance which cannot be accommodated in the general education setting.

courses.description: The ‘Life Skills’ Program is a specialized placement for students with significant intellectual disabilities who need opportunities to develop functional academic skills; along with skills that they will need in everyday life such as: self-care, vocational, functional reading and math, money management, self-advocacy, independence, and others. Placement into the ‘Life Skills’ Program is an IEP team decision and is based on specific student needs and discussion regarding the placement that can meet those needs most appropriately. Placement in the ‘Life Skills’ Program is a decision that is considered yearly by the IEP team. The decision is made after a thorough review of the IEP components which may include present levels of performance, goals/objectives, accommodations, modifications, supplementary aids and services, state and district assessments, behavior intervention plans, teacher and parental input, and results from any previous evaluations.
courses.prerequisites: Must be specified in the Individualized Education Plan.

courses.description: This course is designed to help students develop the necessary skills for independent living. Students will have the opportunity to plan nutritional meals, prepare foods and maintain a kitchen. This course may also contain hand sewing, basic mending and housekeeping skills as well as basic instruction in the following areas: hygiene, health and wellness, family life and sex education, drug and alcohol information, and first aid.
courses.prerequisites: Must be specified in the Individualized Education Plan.

courses.description: This course is designed to help students develop skills which will allow them to work cooperatively in a group, as well as, interact appropriately with peers, adults, and authority figures in a variety of settings.
courses.prerequisites: Must be specified in the Individualized Education Plan.

courses.description: Tier three level practicum provides students with opportunities to apply soft-skills required for effective job performance and career readiness according to the goals specified in the IEP. Students in this course will work on applying the following soft skills: critical thinking and problem solving, teamwork, communication and collaboration, organization, self-awareness and self-advocacy. This course provides alternative credit towards meeting the graduation requirements.
courses.prerequisites: Must be specified in the Individualized Education Plan.
courses.fulfills_text: This course provides alternative credit towards meeting the graduation requirements.

courses.description: Currently, BFUHS offers two classes in-house for both high school credit and college credit. Our Advanced Placement Calculus course can earn a student college credit through River Valley Community College. Credit through Community College of Vermont can be obtained through successful completion of the following courses: Honors American Literature, and 21st Century Writing. Students can also earn Dual Enrollment credit by successfully completing courses taken at colleges and universities, with prior approval from the school administration. Students have the option to take courses at colleges/universities as a level 4-Honors or unleveled. This must be figured out with their school counselor.
courses.provider: CCV / River Valley Community College / other colleges

courses.description: Qualified students can spend their senior year of high school as a fully enrolled college student, thus finishing their requirements for their high school diploma while also completing their first year in college.

Students can make progress toward earning a high school diploma by earning credit through “on-the-job” experiences. Our School Counseling Department has a School Counselor who is tasked with helping students create a work based experience that meets the needs of the student and the workplace ,while demonstrating sufficient documented new learning to earn credit toward graduation. While this learning opportunity is available to all students, based upon their interest and available work experiences, these experiences are most commonly accessed by (1) Special Education students, and (2) students who access one of our two career centers.

Bellows Falls Union High School is pleased to offer Vermont Virtual Learning Cooperative (VTVLC) online courses for students as a piece of the Flexible Pathways Initiative (online courses from other accredited schools are used on a case by case basis). Online learning requires that students learn independently and skills such as initiative, self advocacy, time management, and organization are very important for success. While online courses provide increased educational options and flexibility, it is imperative for students to know that taking an online course is a significant commitment. ** All final online course grades (passing or failing) are officially reported on the transcript and affect a student’s overall GPA.** Students interested in taking an online course should first discuss this with their counselor. Students and parents must sign the Online Student Course Contract before being enrolled in an online course.

courses.course_name: Vermont Adult Learning High School Completion Program
courses.description: Students can earn a BFUHS Diploma by completing a VT Adult Learning High School Completion Program plan, which is created in collaboration with the student (and family), a representative of Vermont Adult Learning and a representative of the high school. This plan can include a wide variety of learning experiences and may or may not include coursework at BFUHS. Similar plans can also be created “in-house” at BFUHS when needed through a student’s PLP.
